claim: TRIP13 is primarily expressed in testis but detected at low levels in ovary and liver
source: TRIP13 was primarily expressed in testis but detected at low levels in ovary and liver (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: TRIP13 is prominent in the cytoplasm of primary spermatocytes, especially leptotene and zygotene cells
source: In the testis, TRIP13 was prominent in the cytoplasm of primary spermatocytes, especially leptotene and zygotene cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B

claim: TRIP13 localizes to telomeres from leptotene to diplotene cells
source: Indeed, we found that TRIP13 localized to telomeres from leptotene to diplotene cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data of surface spread nuclei shown in Figure 1C

claim: TRIP13 localizes to the SC in early pachytene spermatocytes but disappears from the SC in the mid to late pachytene spermatocytes
source: Strikingly, we found that, in addition to telomeres, TRIP13 localized to the SC in early pachytene spermatocytes but disappeared from the SC in the mid to late pachytene spermatocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C

claim: TRIP13 localizes to the SC central region in contrast to the lateral element marker SYCP3
source: In contrast to the lateral element marker SYCP3, TRIP13 localized to the SC central region (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal immunofluorescent microscopy with super-resolution deconvolution shown in Figure 1D

claim: TRIP13 localizes strongly to meiotic telomeres in all stages of prophase I in oocytes, but not as filaments on the SC
source: TRIP13 localized strongly to meiotic telomeres in all stages of prophase I, but not as filaments on the SC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in oocytes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Interbreeding of Trip13+/- mice produced fewer Trip13-/- offspring than expected
source: Interbreeding of Trip13+/- mice produced fewer Trip13-/- offspring than expected: Trip13+/+, 80; Trip13+/-, 220; Trip13-/-, 51 (χ2 = 27, p=0.0001).
evidence: Supported by breeding data with statistical analysis showing significant deviation from expected Mendelian ratios

claim: The body weight of 2–3-month-old males was not significantly different between wild type and Trip13-/- mice
source: The body weight of 2–3-month-old males was not significantly different between wild type (24.3 ± 2.8 g, n = 5) and Trip13-/- mice (22.8 ± 1.7 g, n = 5, p=0.3, Student's t-test).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements with statistical analysis

claim: The Trip13-/- testis was much smaller than Trip13+/- testis
source: The Trip13-/- testis was much smaller than Trip13+/- testis (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by visual comparison shown in Figure 2A

claim: TRIP13 was present in reduced abundance in Trip13+/- testis and not detected in Trip13-/- testis
source: Western blot analysis showed that TRIP13 was present in reduced abundance in Trip13+/- testis and not detected in Trip13-/- testis, demonstrating that this mutant allele is null (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The abundance of SYCP3 was reduced in Trip13-/- testis, suggesting a partial depletion of meiotic cells
source: The abundance of SYCP3, a component of the SC, was also reduced in Trip13-/- testis, suggesting a partial depletion of meiotic cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B; inference made from reduced SYCP3 levels

claim: The testis weight of adult Trip13-/- males was reduced by 74% in comparison with the wild type males
source: The testis weight of adult Trip13-/- males was reduced by 74% in comparison with the wild type males (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by testis weight measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: Adult Trip13-/- males lacked sperm in the epididymis
source: Adult Trip13-/- males lacked sperm in the epididymis (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Trip13-/- testis displayed complete meiotic arrest, evidenced by the presence of early spermatocytes and a lack of secondary spermatocytes, round spermatids, and mature sperm
source: Histological analysis showed that while spermatocytes in all stages of meiosis were present in adult Trip13+/+ and Trip13+/- testes, Trip13-/- testis displayed complete meiotic arrest, evidenced by the presence of early spermatocytes and a lack of secondary spermatocytes, round spermatids, and mature sperm (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Trip13-/- females were sterile
source: Trip13-/- females were also sterile.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study

claim: The adult Trip13-/- ovary was very small and showed a complete loss of oocytes
source: The adult Trip13-/- ovary was very small and showed a complete loss of oocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: About half of the Trip13-/- spermatocytes were in the early pachytene stage and no cells were found at later stages of prophase I
source: While the P20 wild type testis contained spermatocytes from leptotene through diplotene stages, about half of the Trip13-/- spermatocytes were in the early pachytene stage and no cells were found at later stages of prophase I, showing meiotic blockade at the early pachytene stage in Trip13-/- testes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by nuclear spread analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The early pachytene-like spermatocytes from Trip13-/- testes contained unsynapsed chromosomal ends
source: The early pachytene-like spermatocytes from Trip13-/- testes contained unsynapsed chromosomal ends (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 94% of unsynapsed ends were centromeric ends
source: Co-staining with the centromere marker CREST showed that 94% of unsynapsed ends were centromeric ends (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by co-staining data shown in Figure 4A

claim: XY chromosomes were synapsed at the pseudoautosomal regions and thus were connected in wild type and Trip13+/- pachytene spermatocytes
source: While XY chromosomes were synapsed at the pseudoautosomal regions and thus were connected in wild type and Trip13+/- pachytene spermatocytes, they were separate in Trip13-/- pachytene-like spermatocytes (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: XY chromosomes were separate in Trip13-/- pachytene-like spermatocytes
source: While XY chromosomes were synapsed at the pseudoautosomal regions and thus were connected in wild type and Trip13+/- pachytene spermatocytes, they were separate in Trip13-/- pachytene-like spermatocytes (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: SYCE1 localized to the synapsed SC but not to unsynapsed regions in Trip13-/- pachytene-like cells
source: We found that SYCE1, a component of the SC central element, localized to the synapsed SC but not to unsynapsed regions in Trip13-/- pachytene-like cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Many homologous chromosomes in Trip13-/- spermatocytes had split ends and some had regions of interstitial asynapsis
source: Confocal microscopy with super-resolution deconvolution confirmed that many homologous chromosomes in Trip13-/- spermatocytes had split ends and some had regions of interstitial asynapsis (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by super-resolution confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3D

claim: Global loss of Trip13 caused similar defects in autosomal synapsis but a more severe defect in sex chromosome synapsis compared to Trip13 hypomorph mutants
source: Here we found that global loss of Trip13 caused similar defects in autosomal synapsis but a more severe defect in sex chromosome synapsis.
evidence: Comparison with previously reported Trip13 hypomorph mutants (Li and Schimenti, 2007; Roig et al., 2010)

claim: Trip13+/- males were fertile
source: Although Trip13+/- males were fertile, their testis weight and sperm count were significantly reduced in comparison with wild type (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Stated as an observation; supported by testis weight and sperm count data in Figures 2C and 2D

claim: Trip13+/- males had significantly reduced testis weight and sperm count in comparison with wild type
source: Although Trip13+/- males were fertile, their testis weight and sperm count were significantly reduced in comparison with wild type (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by testis weight and sperm count data shown in Figures 2C and 2D

claim: The percentage of spermatocytes with defects in synapsis was higher in Trip13+/- males than wild type
source: The percentage of spermatocytes with defects in synapsis was higher in Trip13+/- males than wild type (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The percentage of spermatocytes with asynapsed XY chromosomes was significantly higher in Trip13+/- males than wild type
source: In addition, the percentage of spermatocytes with asynapsed XY chromosomes was significantly higher in Trip13+/- males than wild type (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G

claim: TRIP13 is a dosage-sensitive regulator of meiosis
source: These results demonstrate that TRIP13 regulates meiosis in a dosage-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Trip13+/- mice show intermediate phenotypes between wild type and Trip13-/- mice

claim: CREST and CENPC still localized to centromeres in Trip13-/- spermatocytes
source: CREST and CENPC still localized to centromeres in Trip13-/- spermatocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: Two CREST or two CENPC foci were observed at the split ends in Trip13-/- spermatocytes
source: Because many Trip13-/- spermatocytes had split ends, two CREST or two CENPC foci were observed at the split ends.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: TRF1 and MAJIN localized to telomeres in Trip13-/- spermatocytes
source: Both TRF1 and MAJIN localized to telomeres in Trip13-/- spermatocytes (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4C and 4D

claim: Two TRF1 or two MAJIN foci were observed at split ends of chromosomes in Trip13-/- spermatocytes
source: As expected, two TRF1 or two MAJIN foci were observed at split ends of chromosomes in Trip13-/- spermatocytes (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4C and 4D

claim: REC114 still formed foci (one per chromosome) on the unsynapsed X and Y chromosomes in Trip13-/- pachytene-like spermatocytes
source: REC114 still formed foci (one per chromosome) on the unsynapsed X and Y chromosomes in Trip13-/- pachytene-like spermatocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: TRIP13 is not required for recruitment of centromere or telomere proteins
source: Taken together, these results suggest that TRIP13 is not required for recruitment of these centromere or telomere proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CREST, CENPC, TRF1, and MAJIN still localize normally in Trip13-/- spermatocytes

claim: HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localize to unsynapsed and desynapsed chromosomes in wild type meiotic cells
source: In wild type meiotic cells, HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localize to unsynapsed and desynapsed chromosomes (Fukuda et al., 2010; Kogo et al., 2012a; Shin et al., 2010; Wojtasz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localized to the largely unsynapsed XY but not to synapsed autosomal SCs in wild type cells
source: Thus, HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localized to the largely unsynapsed XY but not to synapsed autosomal SCs in wild type cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: TRIP13 is essential for removing meiotic HORMADs from the chromosome axes, a function that is conserved in yeast, worms, and mammals
source: TRIP13 is essential for removing meiotic HORMADs from the chromosome axes, a function that is conserved in yeast, worms, and mammals (Wojtasz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 remained on the synapsed autosomes in Trip13-/- pachytene cells
source: We confirmed that HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 remained on the synapsed autosomes in Trip13-/- pachytene cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localize to the interior of the lateral elements in the SC
source: HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localize to the interior of the lateral elements in the SC (Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localized to the lateral elements of the synapsed autosomes in Trip13-/- spermatocytes
source: Confocal microscopy with super-resolution deconvolution revealed that HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 localized to the lateral elements of the synapsed autosomes in Trip13-/- spermatocytes (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by super-resolution imaging shown in Figures 5C and 5D

claim: TRIP13 is essential for HORMAD1/2 removal from the synapsed SCs
source: Our analysis of Trip13-null mutant confirmed that TRIP13 is essential for HORMAD1/2 removal from the synapsed SCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HORMAD1/2 persist on synapsed SCs in Trip13-/- spermatocytes

claim: HORMAD1 is not required for localization of TRIP13 to the SC
source: In both wild type and Hormad1-/- cells, TRIP13 localized to the synapsed regions and to the telomeres (Figure 6A). This result shows that HORMAD1 is not required for localization of TRIP13 to the SC.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Hormad1-/- spermatocytes shown in Figure 6A

claim: In Rec8-/- spermatocytes, TRIP13 localized to synapsed sister chromatids
source: In Rec8-/- spermatocytes, TRIP13 localized to synapsed sister chromatids (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B

claim: TRIP13 localized as filaments in Sycp2-/- spermatocytes, strongly suggesting that its localization is independent of SYCP3 and the C-terminus of SYCP2
source: TRIP13 localized as filaments in Sycp2-/- spermatocytes, strongly suggesting that its localization is independent of SYCP3 and the C-terminus of SYCP2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C; inference made from localization pattern

claim: TRIP13 still localized to the synapsed regions in Skp1cKO spermatocytes
source: We found that TRIP13 still localized to the synapsed regions in Skp1cKO (conditional knockout) spermatocytes (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The SC localization of TRIP13 is independent of HORMAD1, REC8, SYCP2, SYCP3, and SKP1
source: Taken together, these results show that the SC localization of TRIP13 is independent of HORMAD1, REC8, SYCP2, SYCP3, and SKP1, which all localize to the SC lateral elements.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TRIP13 localizes to SC in mutants lacking these proteins

claim: The SC localization of TRIP13 being independent of lateral element proteins is consistent with the localization of TRIP13 to the SC central region
source: Such a finding is consistent with the localization of TRIP13 to the SC central region (Figure 1D).
evidence: Logical inference connecting the independence from lateral element proteins to the central region localization

claim: TRIP13 exists in two isoforms in wild type testis
source: Western blot showed that TRIP13 existed in two isoforms in wild type (non-tagged) testis (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: The major TRIP13 isoform was 50 kDa
source: The major TRIP13 isoform was 50 kDa.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: The minor TRIP13 isoform was slightly larger than 50 kDa
source: The minor isoform was slightly larger than 50 kDa.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: Both FLAG-tagged TRIP13 fusion proteins existed in two isoforms in the homozygous testes
source: Both FLAG-tagged TRIP13 fusion proteins also existed in two isoforms in the homozygous testes, suggesting that they corresponded to the two wild type isoforms.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: The FLAG-tagged TRIP13 proteins localize to both telomeres and SC in pachytene spermatocytes
source: Immunofluorescence analysis using anti-FLAG antibody showed that the FLAG-tagged TRIP13 proteins, like wild type TRIP13, localized to both telomeres and SC in pachytene spermatocytes from both FLAG/FLAG homozygous testes (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Both N- and C-terminally tagged homozygous mice were fertile
source: Importantly, both N- and C-terminally tagged homozygous mice were fertile.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study

claim: Both N- and C-terminal tagged TRIP13 proteins localize normally and are functional
source: These results demonstrate that both N- and C-terminal tagged TRIP13 proteins localize normally and are functional.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that tagged proteins localize like wild type and homozygous mice are fertile

claim: HORMAD2 was enriched in tagged TRIP13 IP
source: HORMAD2, a known TRIP13 substrate protein, was also enriched in tagged TRIP13 IP (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1

claim: A large number of RNA-binding proteins involved in RNA splicing were highly enriched in tagged TRIP13 IP: DDX46, PUF60, RBM25, RBM39, U2AF1, U2AF2, and SRSF11
source: Intriguingly, a large number of RNA-binding proteins involved in RNA splicing were highly enriched in tagged TRIP13 IP: DDX46, PUF60, RBM25, RBM39, U2AF1, U2AF2, and SRSF11 (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1

claim: TRIP13/Pch2 and HORMA domain proteins have mutually exclusive localization patterns on the meiotic chromosome axes
source: Therefore, TRIP13/Pch2 and HORMA domain proteins have mutually exclusive localization patterns on the meiotic chromosome axes, providing an explanation for the depletion of HORMA domain proteins from the synapsed chromosomes in diverse organisms.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TRIP13 localizes to synapsed SC while HORMADs are depleted from synapsed regions

claim: Pch2 localizes to synapsed SC in budding yeast
source: Pch2 has been shown to localize to synapsed SC in budding yeast (Joshi et al., 2009), Caenorhabditis elegans (Deshong et al., 2014; Russo et al., 2023), Arabidopsis (Lambing et al., 2015), and rice (Miao et al., 2013), but not in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Pch2 localizes to synapsed SC in Caenorhabditis elegans
source: Pch2 has been shown to localize to synapsed SC in budding yeast (Joshi et al., 2009), Caenorhabditis elegans (Deshong et al., 2014; Russo et al., 2023), Arabidopsis (Lambing et al., 2015), and rice (Miao et al., 2013), but not in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Pch2 localizes to synapsed SC in Arabidopsis
source: Pch2 has been shown to localize to synapsed SC in budding yeast (Joshi et al., 2009), Caenorhabditis elegans (Deshong et al., 2014; Russo et al., 2023), Arabidopsis (Lambing et al., 2015), and rice (Miao et al., 2013), but not in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Pch2 localizes to synapsed SC in rice
source: Pch2 has been shown to localize to synapsed SC in budding yeast (Joshi et al., 2009), Caenorhabditis elegans (Deshong et al., 2014; Russo et al., 2023), Arabidopsis (Lambing et al., 2015), and rice (Miao et al., 2013), but not in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The transverse filaments are essential for the recruitment of Pch2 to the SC
source: The transverse filaments (TFs) are essential for the recruitment of Pch2 to the SC.
evidence: Supported by evidence from multiple organisms cited in the manuscript

claim: In a budding yeast Zip1 allele with four amino acid substitutions, Pch2 is absent from the SC
source: In a budding yeast Zip1 (encoding the TF component) allele with four amino acid substitutions, Pch2 is absent from the SC (Subramanian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In C. elegans, the TF component SYP-1 is essential for localization of Pch-2 on the paired chromosomes
source: In C. elegans, the TF component SYP-1 is essential for localization of Pch-2 on the paired chromosomes (Deshong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In rice, CRC1 and CEP1 localize to the SC in an inter-dependent manner
source: In rice, CRC1 (Pch2 ortholog) and CEP1 (TF protein) localize to the SC in an inter-dependent manner (Miao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In Arabidopsis, ZYP1 recruits Pch2 to the SC
source: In Arabidopsis, ZYP1 (TF component) recruits Pch2 to the SC (Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Rice CRC1 interacts with CEP1 in the yeast two-hybrid assay
source: In the yeast two-hybrid assay, rice CRC1 interacts with CEP1, Arabidopsis ZYP1 interacts with Pch2, and mouse SYCP1 (TF protein) interacts with TRIP13 (Miao et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Arabidopsis ZYP1 interacts with Pch2 in the yeast two-hybrid assay
source: In the yeast two-hybrid assay, rice CRC1 interacts with CEP1, Arabidopsis ZYP1 interacts with Pch2, and mouse SYCP1 (TF protein) interacts with TRIP13 (Miao et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Mouse SYCP1 interacts with TRIP13 in the yeast two-hybrid assay
source: In the yeast two-hybrid assay, rice CRC1 interacts with CEP1, Arabidopsis ZYP1 interacts with Pch2, and mouse SYCP1 (TF protein) interacts with TRIP13 (Miao et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Loss of SYCP1 in mouse leads to a complete failure in chromosomal synapsis
source: Unlike in other species, loss of SYCP1 (TF protein) in mouse leads to a complete failure in chromosomal synapsis and thus its role in the recruitment of TRIP13 to the synapsed SC cannot be directly addressed (de Vries et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: TRIP13 recruitment is independent of SC axial element proteins REC8 and SYCP2
source: Our findings on the localization of mouse TRIP13 to the SC on the sister chromatids in Rec8-deficient spermatocytes and the short SC stretches in Sycp2 mutant spermatocytes demonstrate that TRIP13 recruitment is independent of SC axial element proteins REC8 and SYCP2 but support the possibility that SYCP1 could recruit TRIP13 to the synapsed SC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TRIP13 localizes to SC in Rec8-/- and Sycp2-/- spermatocytes

claim: SYCP1 could recruit TRIP13 to the synapsed SC
source: Our findings on the localization of mouse TRIP13 to the SC on the sister chromatids in Rec8-deficient spermatocytes and the short SC stretches in Sycp2 mutant spermatocytes demonstrate that TRIP13 recruitment is independent of SC axial element proteins REC8 and SYCP2 but support the possibility that SYCP1 could recruit TRIP13 to the synapsed SC.
evidence: Speculative inference based on data from other organisms and the independence from other SC proteins

claim: The TF protein recruits Pch2/TRIP13 to the SC upon synapsis, which in turn evicts HORMA domain proteins from the synapsed regions
source: These findings lead to the following model: the TF protein recruits Pch2/TRIP13 to the SC upon synapsis, which in turn evicts HORMA domain proteins from the synapsed regions (Figure 7C).
evidence: Model proposed based on data from this study and previous studies

claim: Both TRIP13 and SKP1 are required for the removal of HORMA domain proteins from the synapsed SC
source: Both TRIP13 and SKP1 are required for the removal of HORMA domain proteins from the synapsed SC (Guan et al., 2020; Wojtasz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: SKP1 localizes to the synapsed SC more extensively than TRIP13
source: SKP1 localizes to the synapsed SC more extensively than TRIP13.
evidence: Comparison of localization patterns described in the manuscript

claim: TRIP13 is only detected on the synapsed SC in early pachytene spermatocytes
source: While TRIP13 is only detected on the synapsed SC in early pachytene spermatocytes (Figure 1), SKP1 localizes to the synapsed SC in zygotene, all stages of pachytene, and diplotene spermatocytes (Guan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 and citation to previous study

claim: SKP1 localizes to the synapsed SC in zygotene, all stages of pachytene, and diplotene spermatocytes
source: While TRIP13 is only detected on the synapsed SC in early pachytene spermatocytes (Figure 1), SKP1 localizes to the synapsed SC in zygotene, all stages of pachytene, and diplotene spermatocytes (Guan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: TRIP13 is on CE/TF regions but SKP1 on LEs within the SC
source: The localization of TRIP13 and SKP1 within the SC is different: TRIP13 is on CE/TF regions but SKP1 on LEs.
evidence: Comparison of localization data from this study and previous study

claim: The global level of TRIP13 is reduced in Skp1-deficient testes
source: While the global level of TRIP13 is reduced in Skp1-deficient testes, the localization of TRIP13 and SKP1 to the synapsed SC is independent (Figure 6D; Guan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6D and citation to previous study

claim: The localization of TRIP13 and SKP1 to the synapsed SC is independent
source: While the global level of TRIP13 is reduced in Skp1-deficient testes, the localization of TRIP13 and SKP1 to the synapsed SC is independent (Figure 6D; Guan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6D and citation to previous study

claim: The SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase complex targets HORMAD1 for ubiquitination and degradation in transfected HEK293T cells
source: The SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase complex targets HORMAD1 for ubiquitination and degradation in transfected HEK293T cells (Guan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Loss of TRIP13 leads to the accumulation of HORMAD proteins only to the synapsed SC in pachytene cells
source: Loss of TRIP13 leads to the accumulation of HORMAD proteins only to the synapsed SC in pachytene cells.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 5A and 5B

claim: Depletion of SKP1 causes accumulation of HORMA domain proteins, particularly HORMAD1, on both unsynapsed and synapsed chromosome axes from leptotene through diplotene meiocytes
source: In contrast, depletion of SKP1 causes accumulation of HORMA domain proteins, particularly HORMAD1, on both unsynapsed and synapsed chromosome axes from leptotene through diplotene meiocytes.
evidence: Comparison with previous study on SKP1 function

claim: TRIP13 and SKP1 might regulate different pools of HORMAD proteins in meiocytes
source: Therefore, TRIP13 and SKP1 might regulate different pools of HORMAD proteins in meiocytes (Figure 7C).
evidence: Inferred from the different patterns of HORMAD accumulation in Trip13-/- vs Skp1-deficient meiocytes

claim: In many organisms, including mouse and human, centromeres are the last regions to synapse
source: In many organisms, including mouse and human, centromeres are the last regions to synapse (Bisig et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2005; Qiao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The centromere was proposed to exert an inhibitory effect on synapsis in human cells
source: The centromere was proposed to exert an inhibitory effect on synapsis in human cells (Brown et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Only Skp1 and Trip13 mouse mutants exhibit unsynapsis preferentially at the centromeric end in pachytene-like cells
source: To date, only two mouse mutants (Skp1 and Trip13) exhibit unsynapsis preferentially at the centromeric end in pachytene-like cells.
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes across different mouse mutants

claim: Only Skp1 and Trip13 mouse mutants display abnormal accumulation of HORMAD proteins on the synapsed SC
source: In addition, only these two mouse mutants display abnormal accumulation of HORMAD proteins on the synapsed SC.
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes across different mouse mutants

claim: TRIP13 localizes to telomeres in both spermatocytes and oocytes
source: Intriguingly, TRIP13 localizes to telomeres in both spermatocytes and oocytes.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The centromere is close to one of the telomeres in mouse
source: The centromere is close to one of the telomeres in mouse.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse chromosome structure

claim: The preferential centromeric end asynapsis in Trip13 or Skp1-deficient meiocytes could be related to the abnormal persistence of HORMAD proteins
source: Thus, the preferential centromeric end asynapsis in Trip13 or Skp1-deficient meiocytes could be related to the abnormal persistence of HORMAD proteins.
evidence: Speculative inference connecting TRIP13 telomere localization, centromere proximity, and HORMAD persistence

claim: The dosage-dependent phenotypic variation has been reported in other mouse meiotic mutants such as Tex11, Meiob, and Rnf212
source: The dosage-dependent phenotypic variation has been reported in other mouse meiotic mutants such as Tex11, Meiob, and Rnf212.
evidence: Comparison with other meiotic mutants cited in the manuscript

claim: TEX11 localizes to meiotic chromosomes as foci and regulates crossover formation and chromosome synapsis
source: TEX11 localizes to meiotic chromosomes as foci and regulates crossover formation and chromosome synapsis (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The TEX11 protein levels correlate with genome-wide recombination rates in mice
source: The TEX11 protein levels correlate with genome-wide recombination rates in mice (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: MEIOB is a meiosis-specific ssDNA-binding protein essential for meiotic recombination
source: MEIOB, a meiosis-specific ssDNA-binding protein, is essential for meiotic recombination (Luo et al., 2013; Souquet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In mice with different combinations of Meiob alleles, MEIOB protein levels directly correlate with the severity of meiotic defects
source: In mice with different combinations of Meiob alleles, MEIOB protein levels directly correlate with the severity of meiotic defects (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Sequence variants in human RNF212 are associated with variations in genome-wide recombination rates
source: Sequence variants in human RNF212 are associated with variations in genome-wide recombination rates (Chowdhury et al., 2009; Kong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In mouse, RNF212 forms foci on meiotic chromosomes and regulates crossover formation in a dosage-dependent manner
source: In mouse, RNF212 forms foci on meiotic chromosomes and regulates crossover formation in a dosage-dependent manner (Reynolds et al., 2013).

claim: Dosage sensitivity appears to be a common feature of many regulators of meiosis
